content: The study directly compared EFV to EFV400, with no indirect evidence identified for this comparison. For all other treatment comparisons, except for BIC and RPV, a combination of direct and indirect evidence was available. Both BIC and RPV were retained in the analysis to allow comparisons with the broader therapeutic landscape, but their inclusion did not provide additional information relevant to the comparisons of interest. Summaries of trial characteristics, patient characteristics, and critical appraisal quality assessments are detailed in Appendices E, F, and G, respectively. Regarding trial characteristics, the studies ranged from Phase II to Phase IV, with most being Phase III, double-blinded, and multinational. Baseline characteristics revealed notable differences across trials, particularly in sex distribution, which ranged from all-female to all-male cohorts. Other differences were observed in risk groups and markers of disease severity, but age, sex, CD4 count, and viral load were the most consistently reported and were further explored through meta-regression. Exceptions to low bias risk were limited to open-label trials with high bias risk due to lack of blinding and some recent trials reported only in posters, which lacked sufficient information to determine bias risk with certainty. Results were generally consistent with those from the 2015 review. While no meta-regression adjustments were previously required, one analysis in this review required adjustment for imbalances in the proportion of males, specifically for discontinuations. For all other analyses, the unadjusted model was preferred. Additionally, fixed-effects models were more commonly favored in this review compared to the random-effects models used in 2015, suggesting reduced heterogeneity, possibly due to the exclusion of older treatment nodes. Viral suppression was among the best-reported outcomes, with thresholds such as <50 copies/mL being the most commonly reported. Sensitivity analyses restricting evidence to trials using the <50 copies/mL threshold yielded similar results, supporting the composite approach. Many trials employed the FDA Snapshot algorithm, which considers discontinuations as failures, even in trials that did not explicitly use this approach. Viral suppression, while considered an efficacy outcome, is influenced by tolerability, making it challenging to disentangle these factors when interpreting results. Analyses were restricted to intention-to-treat (ITT) results, though per-protocol results were also analyzed but did not resolve the issue of distinguishing efficacy from tolerability. The analysis of viral suppression at 48 weeks included data from 53 trials with 115 treatment arms and 26,410 patients. Fixed-effects network meta-analysis (NMA) results for comparisons of interest are presented in the study. EFV400 was not statistically distinguishable from standard-dose EFV. At 96 weeks, evidence was derived from 28 trials with 63 treatment arms and 16,495 patients, with similar findings. At 144 weeks, evidence was based on six trials with 13 treatment arms and 5,274 patients. EFV400 data were unavailable at this time point. DTG continued to demonstrate superior viral suppression, though only half of the comparisons were statistically significant, likely due to the smaller number of trials and patients. The network of evidence for changes in CD4 cell counts at 48 weeks included 44 trials with 94 treatment arms and 23,789 patients. Both DTG and EFV400 showed higher estimated increases in CD4 counts compared to most other treatments, though not statistically significant. At 96 weeks, evidence was based on 22 trials with 47 treatment arms and 15,134 patients, with results similar to those at 48 weeks, indicating sustained improvement. At 144 weeks, evidence was based on seven trials with 15 treatment arms and 7,019 patients. The network was sparser at this time point, and EFV400 data were unavailable. The evidence base for mortality in first-line treatment included 21,604 patients across 29 trials with 62 treatment arms. Mortality was considered a critical outcome, but the trials were underpowered for this endpoint. There were 391 deaths in the evidence base, but many comparisons had zero events, rendering estimates unreliable. For example, there were only five deaths each in the DTG and EFV400 groups. Given the small number of events, synthesizing evidence through NMA produced wide credible intervals. No statistically significant differences in mortality outcomes were observed between DTG, EFV, and EFV400. The evidence base for AIDS-defining illnesses (ADIs) included 9,722 patients across 18 trials with 40 treatment arms. Similar issues to those seen in mortality analyses were present, with a small number of events limiting the reliability of estimates. No statistically significant differences in ADI outcomes were observed between DTG, EFV, and EFV400. The evidence base for all-cause discontinuations (retention) included 26,399 patients across 120 treatment arms in 54 trials. This outcome required adjustment for the proportion of males in the trials. DTG was statistically superior to all other treatments except EVG/c, BIC, and DOR, against which it still had a lower estimated rate of discontinuation. The comparison between DTG and EFV400 was based only on indirect evidence, with DTG appearing superior. For discontinuations due to adverse events (AEs), the evidence base included 54 trials with 26,165 patients across 118 treatment arms. Both DTG and EFV400 had the lowest odds of discontinuation due to AEs and were superior to standard-dose EFV. However, DTG and EFV400 were not statistically distinguishable from each other. The evidence for treatment-related adverse events included 15,599 patients across 61 treatment arms in 27 trials, while treatment-emergent adverse events included 18,915 patients across 70 treatment arms in 32 trials. DTG and EFV400 had lower odds of treatment-related AEs compared to other treatments, with DTG having slightly lower odds than EFV400. BIC had the lowest odds of treatment-related AEs overall, followed by DOR, DRV/r, and DTG. Treatments were less distinguishable with respect to emergent AEs. The evidence for treatment-related serious adverse events (SAEs) included 8,041 patients across 31 treatment arms in 15 trials, while treatment-emergent SAEs included 26,706 patients across 98 treatment arms in 45 trials. With only 81 treatment-related SAEs reported, there were too few events to obtain reliable estimates. Treatment-emergent SAEs did not have the same limitation. Neither DTG nor EFV400 distinguished themselves from EFV, though the estimates were lower. The evidence base for regimen substitutions by 48 weeks included 9,263 patients across 18 trials with 41 treatment arms. Results of this analysis did not align with clinical practice, where regimen substitutions are less common with DTG than with EFV. There was no direct evidence supporting the DTG-to-EFV comparison, and very few observed regimen substitutions in the trials. GRADE tables summarizing the quality of evidence for each outcome showed high-quality evidence of improved viral suppression, discontinuations, and discontinuations due to AEs for DTG relative to EFV. Moderate-quality evidence supported improvements in CD4 cell counts and both treatment-related and treatment-emergent AEs. However, evidence for efficacy at 144 weeks, mortality, ADIs, SAEs, and regimen substitutions was of low to very low quality due to imprecise estimates and some risk of bias. For EFV400 relative to standard-dose EFV, high-quality evidence was obtained for discontinuations due to AEs, while other outcomes had moderate-quality evidence. There was no high-quality evidence comparing DTG to EFV400, though moderate evidence suggested DTG led to fewer discontinuations and better long-term viral suppression.
